title: Triangle Inequality Theorem
statement:
In any triangle, the lengths of any two sides add to more than the length of the remaining side.

For triangle \(ABC\), all three strict inequalities hold.
summary: In every triangle, the sum of the lengths of any two sides is greater than the length of the third side.
proofIdea: Extend BA through A to a point D and copy AC onto AD. Then BD is BA + AC. Triangle ACD is isosceles, so its base angles at C and D are congruent. Angle BCD contains angle ACD plus a positive angle, making angle BCD larger than angle BDC. Triangle Side–Angle Order then gives BD > BC, so BA + AC > BC. Relabeling the vertices gives the other two inequalities.
explorationPrompt: Move vertex A and compare each direct side with the two-side route through the remaining vertex. Every two-side route stays longer; the guided construction proves why.

proofSteps.title: Extend and copy
proofSteps.detail: Extend BA through A to a point D, so B–A–D occur in that order. Copy AC onto ray AD, giving AD ≅ AC, and join C to D. Segment addition and substitution give BD = BA + AD = BA + AC.

proofSteps.title: Use the isosceles triangle
proofSteps.detail: Since AD ≅ AC, triangle ACD is isosceles. The Isosceles Base-Angles Theorem gives ∠ACD ≅ ∠CDA. Because B, A, and D are collinear with A between B and D, rays DA and DB are the same ray, so ∠CDA is the same angle as ∠BDC.

proofSteps.title: Compare the angles
proofSteps.detail: Ray CA lies inside ∠BCD. Angle Addition gives ∠BCD = ∠BCA + ∠ACD. Angle ∠BCA has positive size, so ∠BCD > ∠ACD. Together with ∠ACD ≅ ∠BDC, this gives ∠BCD > ∠BDC.

proofSteps.title: Compare the opposite sides
proofSteps.detail: In triangle BCD, the larger angle ∠BCD lies opposite BD, while ∠BDC lies opposite BC. Triangle Side–Angle Order gives BD > BC. Since BD = BA + AC, substitution gives BA + AC > BC. Segments BA and AB are the same side, so this is AB + AC > BC.

proofSteps.title: Relabel the triangle
proofSteps.detail: The choice of BC as the remaining side was arbitrary. Applying the same argument after cycling the vertex names gives AB + BC > AC and AC + BC > AB. Thus the sum of any two side lengths is greater than the third side.

historicalContext.title: Euclid I.20 and the shortest-path principle
paragraphs: Euclid's Proposition I.20 proves that any two sides of a triangle are together greater than the remaining side. Its extension-and-isosceles construction is the argument used in this lesson.

Repeated triangle inequalities express a broad shortest-path principle: a broken route cannot beat the direct distance. An analogous non-strict inequality is part of what defines distance in a metric space and governs length in normed vector spaces.

The inequality is strict for triangle ABC because its three vertices are not collinear. Equality can occur only at the straight-line boundary, when the intermediate point lies on a direct shortest route; that boundary is not a triangle.
